claim: Genetic techniques enabling conditional analysis of gene function are limited in zebrafish despite its extensive use as a model organism in developmental biology and regeneration research.
source: Despite the extensive use of zebrafish as a model organism in developmental biology and regeneration research, genetic techniques enabling conditional analysis of gene function are limited.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as a motivation for the study.

claim: Zwitch is a Cre-dependent invertible gene-trap cassette that enables the establishment of conditional alleles in zebrafish by generating intronic insertions via in vivo homologous recombination.
source: In this study, we generated Zwitch, a Cre-dependent invertible gene-trap cassette, enabling the establishment of conditional alleles in zebrafish by generating intronic insertions via in vivo homologous recombination.
evidence: The authors describe the generation and function of Zwitch in the abstract.

claim: Homozygous shha mutants generated using Zwitch developed normally in the absence of Cre expression.
source: Homozygous shha mutants developed normally; however, shha mutant embryos globally expressing Cre exhibited strong reductions in endogenous shha and shha target gene mRNA levels and developmental defects associated with null shha mutations.
evidence: The abstract states that homozygous shha mutants developed normally without Cre activation.

claim: shha mutant embryos globally expressing Cre exhibited strong reductions in endogenous shha and shha target gene mRNA levels.
source: Homozygous shha mutants developed normally; however, shha mutant embryos globally expressing Cre exhibited strong reductions in endogenous shha and shha target gene mRNA levels and developmental defects associated with null shha mutations.
evidence: The abstract describes the effect of Cre expression on shha mutant embryos.

claim: shha mutant embryos globally expressing Cre exhibited developmental defects associated with null shha mutations.
source: Homozygous shha mutants developed normally; however, shha mutant embryos globally expressing Cre exhibited strong reductions in endogenous shha and shha target gene mRNA levels and developmental defects associated with null shha mutations.
evidence: The abstract describes developmental defects in Cre-expressing shha mutants.

claim: Epicardium-derived Shha plays unique roles in myocardial proliferation during heart development.
source: Analyzing a conditional shha mutant generated using an epicardium-specific inducible Cre driver revealed unique roles for epicardium-derived Shha in myocardial proliferation during heart development and regeneration.
evidence: The abstract states that epicardium-specific conditional analysis revealed unique roles for Shha in myocardial proliferation during development.

claim: Epicardium-derived Shha plays unique roles in myocardial proliferation during heart regeneration.
source: Analyzing a conditional shha mutant generated using an epicardium-specific inducible Cre driver revealed unique roles for epicardium-derived Shha in myocardial proliferation during heart development and regeneration.
evidence: The abstract states that epicardium-specific conditional analysis revealed unique roles for Shha in myocardial proliferation during regeneration.

claim: Zwitch will extend the utility of zebrafish in organ development and regeneration research.
source: Zwitch will extend the utility of zebrafish in organ development and regeneration research and might be applicable to other model organisms.
evidence: The abstract concludes with this statement about the potential utility of Zwitch.

claim: Zwitch might be applicable to other model organisms.
source: Zwitch will extend the utility of zebrafish in organ development and regeneration research and might be applicable to other model organisms.
evidence: The abstract suggests potential applicability to other organisms.

claim: Conditional gene knockout (cKO) enables the investigation of gene function in a temporally regulated manner in specific tissues or cell types.
source: Conditional gene knockout (cKO) is a genetic technique that enables the investigation of gene function in a temporally regulated manner in specific tissues or cell types (Lobe and Nagy, 1998; Rajewsky et al., 1996; Rossant and McMahon, 1999).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: A conditional approach is often essential for deciphering the tissue-specific function of a gene in later biological events, avoiding the confounding effects of embryonic lethality or other morphogenetic defects that can result from global gene deletion.
source: Although the global KO approach is useful for investigating the first developmental function of a gene of interest, a conditional approach is often essential for deciphering the tissue-specific function of a gene in later biological events, avoiding the confounding effects of embryonic lethality or other morphogenetic defects that can result from global gene deletion.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a rationale for conditional approaches.

claim: The cKO approach has been used most extensively in mice, owing to the availability of embryonic stem (ES) cells.
source: The cKO approach has been used most extensively in mice, owing to the availability of embryonic stem (ES) cells.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction.

claim: ES cells possess the unique capacity of efficient homologous recombination (HR) (Koller and Smithies, 1992; Thomas and Capecchi, 1987).
source: ES cells possess the unique capacity of efficient homologous recombination (HR) (Koller and Smithies, 1992; Thomas and Capecchi, 1987), thereby providing a platform for engineering loxP-flanking (floxed) genomic segments that can be excised by Cre recombinase.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: ES cells provide a platform for engineering loxP-flanking (floxed) genomic segments that can be excised by Cre recombinase.
source: ES cells possess the unique capacity of efficient homologous recombination (HR) (Koller and Smithies, 1992; Thomas and Capecchi, 1987), thereby providing a platform for engineering loxP-flanking (floxed) genomic segments that can be excised by Cre recombinase.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a consequence of ES cell properties.

claim: Recent advances in genome editing technologies have provided new possibilities for efficiently engineering conditional alleles in any model organism without the need for ES cells (Bedell et al., 2012; Brown et al., 2013; Dickinson et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2013).
source: However, recent advances in genome editing technologies have provided new possibilities for efficiently engineering conditional alleles in any model organism without the need for ES cells (Bedell et al., 2012; Brown et al., 2013; Dickinson et al., 2013; Wang et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: The first floxed allele of an endogenous zebrafish gene generated using transcription activator-like effector nuclease (TALEN)-mediated HR was only recently reported (Hoshijima et al., 2016).
source: However, the first floxed allele of an endogenous zebrafish gene generated using transcription activator-like effector nuclease (TALEN)-mediated HR was only recently reported (Hoshijima et al., 2016).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: FLEx is characterized by strategically arranged wild-type (WT) and mutant loxP sites that facilitate the induction of Cre-dependent stable inversion of a gene trap cassette (Schnütgen et al., 2003).
source: FLEx is characterized by strategically arranged wild-type (WT) and mutant loxP sites that facilitate the induction of Cre-dependent stable inversion of a gene trap cassette (Schnütgen et al., 2003).
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with a supporting citation.

claim: Similar approaches to FLEx have been used for conditional gene trap mutagenesis in zebrafish (Clark et al., 2011; Ni et al., 2012; Jungke et al., 2016; Trinh et al., 2011).
source: Although similar approaches have been used for conditional gene trap mutagenesis in zebrafish (Clark et al., 2011; Ni et al., 2012; Jungke et al., 2016; Trinh et al., 2011), no reports have described the precise targeting of a FLEx cassette at defined loci.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction with supporting citations.

claim: No reports have described the precise targeting of a FLEx cassette at defined loci in zebrafish prior to this study.
source: Although similar approaches have been used for conditional gene trap mutagenesis in zebrafish (Clark et al., 2011; Ni et al., 2012; Jungke et al., 2016; Trinh et al., 2011), no reports have described the precise targeting of a FLEx cassette at defined loci.
evidence: This is stated in the introduction as a gap in the literature.

claim: Zwitch was modified from FT1 (Ni et al., 2012), a FLEx construct used for random gene trap mutagenesis in zebrafish.
source: We modified FT1 (Ni et al., 2012), a FLEx construct used for random gene trap mutagenesis in zebrafish, and generated a donor vector for the generation of zebrafish with an invertible gene trap cassette via HR (Zwitch) (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the generation of Zwitch.

claim: Zwitch consists of a removable, lens-specific enhanced green fluorescence protein (EGFP) tag (LG) (Lee et al., 2005).
source: Zwitch consists of a removable, lens-specific enhanced green fluorescence protein (EGFP) tag (LG) (Lee et al., 2005) and an invertible splice acceptor site conjugated to a gene expressing a red fluorescent protein (TagRFP) via a 2A self-cleaving peptide sequence (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the components of Zwitch.

claim: Zwitch consists of an invertible splice acceptor site conjugated to a gene expressing a red fluorescent protein (TagRFP) via a 2A self-cleaving peptide sequence.
source: Zwitch consists of a removable, lens-specific enhanced green fluorescence protein (EGFP) tag (LG) (Lee et al., 2005) and an invertible splice acceptor site conjugated to a gene expressing a red fluorescent protein (TagRFP) via a 2A self-cleaving peptide sequence (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the components of Zwitch.

claim: The region encompassing LG and the gene trap cassette in Zwitch is flanked by unique restriction enzyme sites in which the right arm (RA) and left arm (LA) of homologous sequences are inserted.
source: The region encompassing LG and the gene trap cassette is flanked by unique restriction enzyme sites in which the right arm (RA) and left arm (LA) of homologous sequences are inserted (Figure 1A and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the structure of Zwitch.

claim: The TALEN pair used for shha targeting induced DNA double-strand breaks with 67% efficiency.
source: The efficiency of the TALEN pair in inducing DSBs (67%) was quantified from the gel image using ImageJ software.
evidence: Figure 1C shows the quantification of TALEN efficiency.

claim: 19 out of 32 LG+ potential founders (59%) transmitted LG expression.
source: We screened 32 LG+ potential founders, finding that 19 of them (59%) transmitted LG expression (Figure 1E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the screening process.

claim: Zwitch was inserted in the correct non-mutagenic orientation in 17 out of 19 (89%) LG+ founders.
source: PCR demonstrated that Zwitch was inserted in the correct non-mutagenic orientation in 17 (89%) of the 19 LG+ founders (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the screening results.

claim: Genomic PCR and reverse transcription (RT)-PCR detected the gene trap cassette inversion and alternative shha splicing in embryos injected with Cre DNA (Cre+) but not in uninjected embryos (Cre−).
source: Genomic PCR and reverse transcription (RT)-PCR detected the gene trap cassette inversion (Figure 2B) and alternative shha splicing in embryos injected with Cre DNA (Cre+) but not in uninjected embryos (Cre−) (Figure 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the characterization of the shhact allele.

claim: DNA sequencing verified the precise inversion of the gene trap cassette.
source: DNA sequencing verified the precise inversion (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A) and in-frame transcription of shha-P2A-TagRFP mRNA (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the verification of cassette inversion.

claim: DNA sequencing verified in-frame transcription of shha-P2A-TagRFP mRNA.
source: DNA sequencing verified the precise inversion (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A) and in-frame transcription of shha-P2A-TagRFP mRNA (Figure 2—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the verification of mRNA transcription.

claim: Flp mRNA injection induced excision of the FRT-flanked LG cassette.
source: We injected Flp mRNA into one-cell-stage embryos of the offspring of an incross of shhact/+ fish and detected the excision of the FRT-flanked LG cassette using genomic PCR (Figure 2D and E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing Flp-mediated excision.

claim: EGFP fluorescence was lost or reduced at approximately the expected frequency of the homozygous or heterozygous shhact genotype after Flp injection.
source: EGFP fluorescence was lost or reduced at approximately the expected frequency of the homozygous or heterozygous shhact genotype (Figure 2F and G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the effect of Flp injection on EGFP expression.

claim: The expression of shha and Hedgehog (Hh) target genes was strongly decreased in Cre+shhact/ct embryos but not in Cre− shhact/ct embryos.
source: Quantitative RT-PCR (qRT-CPR) revealed that the expression of shha and Hedgehog (Hh) target genes was strongly decreased in Cre+shhact/ct embryos but not in Cre− shhact/ct embryos, indicating that the shhact allele is functional in the absence of Cre activation (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section validating the loss-of-function nature of the shhact allele.

claim: The shhact allele is functional in the absence of Cre activation.
source: Quantitative RT-PCR (qRT-CPR) revealed that the expression of shha and Hedgehog (Hh) target genes was strongly decreased in Cre+shhact/ct embryos but not in Cre− shhact/ct embryos, indicating that the shhact allele is functional in the absence of Cre activation (Figure 3A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the qRT-PCR data.

claim: Most Cre+ shhact/ct embryos exhibited truncated pectoral fins and U-shaped somites that lacked clear horizontal myosepta.
source: Furthermore, most Cre+ shhact/ct embryos exhibited truncated pectoral fins and U-shaped somites that lacked clear horizontal myosepta (Figure 3B and C), defects reminiscent of homozygous shha mutant embryos (Schauerte et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the phenotype of Cre+ shhact/ct embryos.

claim: The defects observed in Cre+ shhact/ct embryos are reminiscent of homozygous shha mutant embryos (Schauerte et al., 1998).
source: Furthermore, most Cre+ shhact/ct embryos exhibited truncated pectoral fins and U-shaped somites that lacked clear horizontal myosepta (Figure 3B and C), defects reminiscent of homozygous shha mutant embryos (Schauerte et al., 1998).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section comparing the observed phenotype to published data.

claim: Pectoral fin development was largely normal in WT and heterozygous mutant embryos but severely hampered in all homozygous mutants examined.
source: We found that pectoral fin development was largely normal in WT and heterozygous mutant embryos but severely hampered in all homozygous mutants examined (Figure 3—figure supplement 2C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the analysis of ubb:Cre-GFP; shhact embryos.

claim: shha expression was reduced to nearly 50% of WT levels in the heterozygous mutants and to an undetectable level in the homozygous mutants.
source: We also performed semi-qRT-PCR analysis of shha expression and confirmed that its expression was reduced to nearly 50% of WT levels in the heterozygous mutants and to an undetectable level in the homozygous mutants (Figure 3—figure supplement 2D and E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the semi-qRT-PCR analysis.

claim: Zwitch can inducibly disrupt gene function in zebrafish.
source: Together, these results provide clear evidence that Zwitch can inducibly disrupt gene function in zebrafish.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the validation experiments.

claim: shha is expressed in epicardial cells during zebrafish heart development.
source: Using fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS), we purified epicardial cells and cardiomyocytes from the dissected hearts of transgenic reporter fish (see Flow cytometry, Materials and methods) and confirmed shha expression in epicardial cells and ptch1 expression in both epicardial cells and cardiomyocytes (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the analysis of shha expression in purified cells.

claim: ptch1 is expressed in both epicardial cells and cardiomyocytes during zebrafish heart development.
source: Using fluorescence-activated cell sorting (FACS), we purified epicardial cells and cardiomyocytes from the dissected hearts of transgenic reporter fish (see Flow cytometry, Materials and methods) and confirmed shha expression in epicardial cells and ptch1 expression in both epicardial cells and cardiomyocytes (Figure 4A).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the analysis of ptch1 expression in purified cells.

claim: In situ hybridization analysis detected shha expression in the epicardium of the ventricle.
source: In situ hybridization analysis also detected shha expression in the epicardium of the ventricle (Figure 4—figure supplement 1A–C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing in situ hybridization results.

claim: 4-hydroxytamoxifen (4-HT) treatment of tcf21:CreER; shhact/ct embryos from 24–72 hpf induced a nearly complete inversion of the gene trap cassette.
source: We inactivated shha expression in the epicardium by treating 24–72 hr post-fertilization (hpf) embryos with 4-hydroxytamoxifen (4-HT; Figure 4B), which induced a nearly complete inversion of the gene trap cassette (Figure 4—figure supplement 2D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the induction of epicardium-specific shha inactivation.

claim: Most embryos lacking shha expression in the epicardium (epi-KO) developed severe cardiac edema by 96 hpf.
source: Strikingly, most embryos lacking shha expression in the epicardium (epi-KO) developed severe cardiac edema by 96 hpf (Figure 4C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the phenotype of epi-KO embryos.

claim: Cardiac edema was unclear or extremely weak in epi-KO hearts at 72 hpf.
source: Cardiac edema was unclear or extremely weak in epi-KO hearts at 72 hpf, suggesting that epicardial inactivation of shha expression leads to heart defects at later developmental stages.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the timing of cardiac edema development.

claim: Epicardial inactivation of shha expression leads to heart defects at later developmental stages.
source: Cardiac edema was unclear or extremely weak in epi-KO hearts at 72 hpf, suggesting that epicardial inactivation of shha expression leads to heart defects at later developmental stages.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the timing of cardiac edema.

claim: The epi-KO embryos had a thinner myocardial wall.
source: The epi-KO embryos had a thinner myocardial wall (Figure 4D) and significantly fewer cardiomyocytes (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the cardiac phenotype of epi-KO embryos.

claim: The epi-KO embryos had significantly fewer cardiomyocytes.
source: The epi-KO embryos had a thinner myocardial wall (Figure 4D) and significantly fewer cardiomyocytes (Figure 4E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the cardiac phenotype of epi-KO embryos.

claim: Epicardium-derived Shha plays a crucial role in zebrafish heart development.
source: These findings indicate that epicardium-derived Shha plays a crucial role in zebrafish heart development.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the epi-KO phenotype analysis.

claim: The expression of tcf21 and pard3 was normal in epi-KO hearts.
source: To investigate the mechanism underlying the developmental defects in epi-KO hearts, we analyzed the expression of the pan-epicardium markers tcf21 and pard3 using semi-qRT-PCR (Plavicki et al., 2014; Serluca, 2008) and detected the normal expression of these marker genes in epi-KO hearts (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the analysis of epicardial markers.

claim: Epicardium-specific loss of shha does not directly affect the development of the epicardium.
source: This result suggests that epicardium-specific loss of shha does not directly affect the development of the epicardium, consistent with the observation that epicardial development is normal in mutant mouse hearts lacking the Shh receptor smoothened (Rudat et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the normal expression of epicardial markers.

claim: Epicardial development is normal in mutant mouse hearts lacking the Shh receptor smoothened (Rudat et al., 2013).
source: This result suggests that epicardium-specific loss of shha does not directly affect the development of the epicardium, consistent with the observation that epicardial development is normal in mutant mouse hearts lacking the Shh receptor smoothened (Rudat et al., 2013).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as supporting evidence from the literature.

claim: The expression of raldh2/aldh1a2 was strongly decreased in epi-KO hearts.
source: However, the expression of the well-characterized epicardial marker raldh2/aldh1a2, which encodes an enzyme that plays a key role in retinoic acid (RA) synthesis (Begemann et al., 2001; Cunningham and Duester, 2015; Niederreither et al., 1999; Sucov and Evans, 1995), was strongly decreased (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the analysis of raldh2 expression.

claim: raldh2/aldh1a2 encodes an enzyme that plays a key role in retinoic acid (RA) synthesis (Begemann et al., 2001; Cunningham and Duester, 2015; Niederreither et al., 1999; Sucov and Evans, 1995).
source: However, the expression of the well-characterized epicardial marker raldh2/aldh1a2, which encodes an enzyme that plays a key role in retinoic acid (RA) synthesis (Begemann et al., 2001; Cunningham and Duester, 2015; Niederreither et al., 1999; Sucov and Evans, 1995), was strongly decreased (Figure 4F).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with supporting citations.

claim: DsRed2+ epicardial cells were normally distributed throughout the epi-KO heart.
source: We induced epicardium-specific inactivation of shha expression in these embryos and found that DsRed2+ epicardial cells were normally distributed throughout the epi-KO heart (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the analysis of epicardial cell distribution.

claim: Raldh2 protein expression was barely detectable in mutant DsRed2+ cells.
source: Consistent with the PCR results (Figure 4F), Raldh2 protein expression was barely detectable in mutant DsRed2+ cells (Figure 4G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the immunofluorescence analysis of Raldh2.

claim: Defects in RA synthesis might underlie the developmental defect in epi-KO hearts.
source: These findings suggest that defects in RA synthesis might underlie the developmental defect in epi-KO hearts.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the loss of Raldh2 expression.

claim: The expression of fgf2 and wnt9b was strongly decreased in epi-KO hearts.
source: The expression of fgf2 and wnt9b, two cardiomyocyte mitogens regulated by RA signaling during mouse heart development (Merki et al., 2005), was strongly decreased in epi-KO hearts (Figure 4H), whereas that of igf2a and igf2b, factors regulated by liver-derived erythropoietin (Brade et al., 2011), was unaffected (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the analysis of mitogen expression.

claim: fgf2 and wnt9b are two cardiomyocyte mitogens regulated by RA signaling during mouse heart development (Merki et al., 2005).
source: The expression of fgf2 and wnt9b, two cardiomyocyte mitogens regulated by RA signaling during mouse heart development (Merki et al., 2005), was strongly decreased in epi-KO hearts (Figure 4H), whereas that of igf2a and igf2b, factors regulated by liver-derived erythropoietin (Brade et al., 2011), was unaffected (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: The expression of igf2a and igf2b was unaffected in epi-KO hearts.
source: The expression of fgf2 and wnt9b, two cardiomyocyte mitogens regulated by RA signaling during mouse heart development (Merki et al., 2005), was strongly decreased in epi-KO hearts (Figure 4H), whereas that of igf2a and igf2b, factors regulated by liver-derived erythropoietin (Brade et al., 2011), was unaffected (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the analysis of mitogen expression.

claim: igf2a and igf2b are factors regulated by liver-derived erythropoietin (Brade et al., 2011).
source: The expression of fgf2 and wnt9b, two cardiomyocyte mitogens regulated by RA signaling during mouse heart development (Merki et al., 2005), was strongly decreased in epi-KO hearts (Figure 4H), whereas that of igf2a and igf2b, factors regulated by liver-derived erythropoietin (Brade et al., 2011), was unaffected (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: The expression of fgf9, fgf20a, and fgf20b was unaffected in epi-KO hearts.
source: Interestingly, the expression of fgf9, a gene encoding a key FGF regulated by RA signaling in the mouse heart (Lavine et al., 2005), as well as fgf20a and fgf20b was unaffected in epi-KO hearts, whereas fgf16 expression levels was strongly decreased (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the analysis of FGF expression.

claim: fgf9 encodes a key FGF regulated by RA signaling in the mouse heart (Lavine et al., 2005).
source: Interestingly, the expression of fgf9, a gene encoding a key FGF regulated by RA signaling in the mouse heart (Lavine et al., 2005), as well as fgf20a and fgf20b was unaffected in epi-KO hearts, whereas fgf16 expression levels was strongly decreased (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: fgf16 expression levels was strongly decreased in epi-KO hearts.
source: Interestingly, the expression of fgf9, a gene encoding a key FGF regulated by RA signaling in the mouse heart (Lavine et al., 2005), as well as fgf20a and fgf20b was unaffected in epi-KO hearts, whereas fgf16 expression levels was strongly decreased (Figure 4H).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the analysis of FGF expression.

claim: Although FGF regulation by RA signals is evolutionary conserved, different FGF proteins may regulate cardiogenesis in zebrafish and mammals.
source: These findings suggest that although FGF regulation by RA signals is evolutionary conserved, different FGF proteins may regulate cardiogenesis in zebrafish and mammals.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as an inference from the differential FGF expression patterns.

claim: fgf2, fgf16, and wnt9b are primarily expressed in the epicardium during zebrafish heart development.
source: We also analyzed the expression of fgf2, fgf16, and wnt9b in purified cardiomyocytes and epicardial cells (Figure 4A), finding that they are primarily expressed in the epicardium during zebrafish heart development (Figure 4I).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the analysis of mitogen expression in purified cells.

claim: Epicardium-specific inactivation of shha expression revealed that Shha plays a crucial role in RA synthesis and mitogen expression in the epicardium during heart development in zebrafish.
source: Thus, epicardium-specific inactivation of shha expression revealed that Shha plays a crucial role in RA synthesis and mitogen expression in the epicardium during heart development in zebrafish.
evidence: This is stated in the Results section as a conclusion from the epi-KO analysis.

claim: Studies using cyclopamine, which globally inhibits Hh signaling, indicated that epicardial Shha promotes myocardial proliferation (Choi et al., 2013).
source: Studies using cyclopamine, which globally inhibits Hh signaling, indicated that epicardial Shha promotes myocardial proliferation (Choi et al., 2013) and epicardial regeneration in cultured injured hearts in vitro (Wang et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: Studies using cyclopamine indicated that epicardial Shha promotes epicardial regeneration in cultured injured hearts in vitro (Wang et al., 2015a).
source: Studies using cyclopamine, which globally inhibits Hh signaling, indicated that epicardial Shha promotes myocardial proliferation (Choi et al., 2013) and epicardial regeneration in cultured injured hearts in vitro (Wang et al., 2015a).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: The shha promoter is activated in regenerating epicardium (Choi et al., 2013).
source: Consistent with the observation that the shha promoter is activated in regenerating epicardium (Choi et al., 2013), we detected shha expression in epicardial cells via in situ hybridization (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–F) and semi-qRT-PCR in purified epicardial cells from tcf21:DsRed2 hearts at 7 days postinjury (dpi) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section with a supporting citation.

claim: shha expression was detected in epicardial cells via in situ hybridization at 7 days postinjury (dpi).
source: Consistent with the observation that the shha promoter is activated in regenerating epicardium (Choi et al., 2013), we detected shha expression in epicardial cells via in situ hybridization (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–F) and semi-qRT-PCR in purified epicardial cells from tcf21:DsRed2 hearts at 7 days postinjury (dpi) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the analysis of shha expression during regeneration.

claim: shha expression was detected by semi-qRT-PCR in purified epicardial cells from tcf21:DsRed2 hearts at 7 days postinjury (dpi).
source: Consistent with the observation that the shha promoter is activated in regenerating epicardium (Choi et al., 2013), we detected shha expression in epicardial cells via in situ hybridization (Figure 4—figure supplement 1D–F) and semi-qRT-PCR in purified epicardial cells from tcf21:DsRed2 hearts at 7 days postinjury (dpi) (Figure 5B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the analysis of shha expression during regeneration.

claim: 4-HT treatment of adult tcf21:DsRed2; tcf21:CreER; shhact/ct fish induced a nearly complete inversion of the gene trap cassette.
source: Next, we analyzed adult tcf21:DsRed2; tcf21:CreER; shhact/ct fish treated with 4-HT, which induced a nearly complete inversion of the gene trap cassette (Figure 4—figure supplement 2E).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the induction of epicardium-specific shha inactivation in adults.

claim: Semi-qRT-PCR confirmed that shha expression was depleted in epicardial cells purified from injured hearts.
source: Semi-qRT-PCR confirmed that shha expression was depleted in epicardial cells purified from injured hearts (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the confirmation of shha depletion.

claim: Unlike the embryonic epi-KO heart, ptch1 and raldh2 expression was unchanged in shha mutant adult hearts.
source: Interestingly, unlike the embryonic epi-KO heart (Figure 4B and F), ptch1 and raldh2 expression was unchanged in shha mutant adult hearts (Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 2A and B).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the analysis of gene expression in adult epi-KO hearts.

claim: Epicardial cells normally infiltrated the injury site in epi-KO hearts.
source: Moreover, epicardial cells normally infiltrated the injury site (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–C) and incorporated 5-ethynyl-2′-deoxyuridine (EdU), a DNA synthesis marker, in epi-KO hearts (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C and D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the analysis of epicardial cell behavior during regeneration.

claim: Epicardial cells incorporated 5-ethynyl-2′-deoxyuridine (EdU), a DNA synthesis marker, in epi-KO hearts.
source: Moreover, epicardial cells normally infiltrated the injury site (Figure 5—figure supplement 2A–C) and incorporated 5-ethynyl-2′-deoxyuridine (EdU), a DNA synthesis marker, in epi-KO hearts (Figure 5—figure supplement 2C and D).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the analysis of epicardial cell proliferation during regeneration.

claim: The expression of dhh and ihhb was detected in epicardial cells purified from injured hearts.
source: Consistent with the previous report (Wang et al., 2015a), we detected the expression of other Hh ligand genes, namely dhh and ihhb, in epicardial cells purified from injured hearts (Figure 5B) and epi-KO hearts (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the analysis of Hh ligand expression.

claim: The expression of dhh and ihhb was detected in epicardial cells purified from epi-KO hearts.
source: Consistent with the previous report (Wang et al., 2015a), we detected the expression of other Hh ligand genes, namely dhh and ihhb, in epicardial cells purified from injured hearts (Figure 5B) and epi-KO hearts (Figure 5C).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the analysis of Hh ligand expression.

claim: Redundant Hh proteins or non-epicardium-derived Shha may play a role in RA synthesis and epicardial regeneration in the adult zebrafish heart.

claim: Myocardial cell proliferation was significantly decreased in the subepicardial area of injured epi-KO hearts.

evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the analysis of myocardial proliferation during regeneration.

claim: Myocardial cell proliferation was not reduced in the trabecular myocardium, an area distant from the epicardium, in epi-KO hearts.

evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the spatial pattern of myocardial proliferation defects.

claim: Epicardial cells and subepicardial cardiomyocytes directly interact during cardiac regeneration.
source: Immunofluorescence analysis of injured tcf21:DsRed2; gata4:EGFP hearts revealed that epicardial cells and subepicardial cardiomyocytes directly interact (Figure 5F), and semi-qRT-PCR analysis revealed that the expression of Hh target genes was strongly induced in gata4:EGFP+ subepicardial cardiomyocytes but not in control cardiomyocytes purified from uninjured Tg(cmlc2:EGFP) (cmlc2:EGFP) hearts (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the analysis of epicardial-myocardial interactions.

claim: The expression of Hh target genes was strongly induced in gata4:EGFP+ subepicardial cardiomyocytes but not in control cardiomyocytes purified from uninjured cmlc2:EGFP hearts.
source: Immunofluorescence analysis of injured tcf21:DsRed2; gata4:EGFP hearts revealed that epicardial cells and subepicardial cardiomyocytes directly interact (Figure 5F), and semi-qRT-PCR analysis revealed that the expression of Hh target genes was strongly induced in gata4:EGFP+ subepicardial cardiomyocytes but not in control cardiomyocytes purified from uninjured Tg(cmlc2:EGFP) (cmlc2:EGFP) hearts (Figure 5G).
evidence: This is stated in the Results section describing the analysis of Hh signaling in subepicardial cardiomyocytes.

claim: Epicardial Shha transmits direct, short-range signals that promote the proliferation of adjacent cardiomyocytes during zebrafish heart regeneration.

The loxP sites were provided by a donor plasmid that expressed the α-crystallin:Venus reporter gene, which was used to identify founders carrying the modified alleles with an overall germline transmission efficiency of 12% (Hoshijima et al., 2016).

claim: Using Zwitch in this study, a germline transmission efficiency of 59% was achieved.

claim: 89% of alleles generated using Zwitch were in the correct non-mutagenic orientation.

claim: Several studies reported the insertion of large DNA fragments at defined zebrafish gene loci via DSB-mediated HR (Hisano et al., 2015; Hoshijima et al., 2016; Shin et al., 2014; Zu et al., 2013).
source: After pioneering studies demonstrated the editing of zebrafish genome with long dsDNA (Bedell et al., 2012; Zu et al., 2013), several studies reported the insertion of large DNA fragments at defined zebrafish gene loci via DSB-mediated HR (Hisano et al., 2015; Hoshijima et al., 2016; Shin et al., 2014; Zu et al., 2013) or homology-independent repair mechanisms (Auer et al., 2014; Kimura et al., 2014; Li et al., 2015).

claim: Several studies reported the insertion of large DNA fragments at defined zebrafish gene loci via homology-independent repair mechanisms (Auer et al., 2014; Kimura et al., 2014; Li et al., 2015).

claim: The variability in the expression of TagRFP might be attributed, at least in part, to inefficient cleavage of the 2A peptide in the target cells.
